newsitem.title: UK: British MP quits Conservatives, attacks Major.
newsitem.headline: British MP quits Conservatives, attacks Major.

text.p: A British member of parliament on Saturday quit the ruling Conservative Party for the small anti-European Referendum Party, accusing Prime Minister John Major of abdicating leadership on the issue of national sovreignty.

In a move exposing once again the rift among Conservatives over future relations with the European Union only weeks before a general election, Sir George Gardiner said he was "sick to death of equivocation over Europe and the single currency".

Gardiner becomes the first MP for the small but vociferous Referendum Party, formed a year ago by millionaire businessman Sir James Goldmsith to give a voice to widespread scepticism in Britain over EU integration.
He is the fourth MP to quit the Conservatives in the past 18 months and his defection put Major's unpopular government into a minority of two in the 651-seat lower house of parliament.

Gardiner, 62, had already fallen out with his constituency's Conservative association over previous remarks likening Major to a ventriloquist's dummy and was de-selected by it as its candidate for the forthcoming election, which must be held no later than May 22.
But political analysts were taken aback by the viciousness of his attack on Major's leadership in a statement on Saturday.

Gardiner accused Major, who supports a "wait and see" policy on British membership of the planned EU single currrency, of an "abdication of national leadership without parallel in the history of Britain over a hundred years".
He attacked Major for "constant fence sitting" and added; "A truly Conservative prime minister would long ago have proclaimed his abhorrence of a single currency -- 1999, 2001 or whenever."
Major has battled against the so-called Eurosceptics throughout his six year stint as prime minister and forced a party leadership contest over the issue in July 1995.

Senior Conservatives sought to play down Gardiner's defection, which hits a party already around 20 percentage points behind the opposition Labour Party in opinion polls ahead of elections expected on May 1.
"I think it is regrettable but I don't think it will have any great national impact," Social Security Secretary Peter Lilley said.
But Sir Teddy Taylor, a Conservative Eurosceptic MP, hoped the move would prompt Major to think again about holding a referendum on the wider issue of European integration.
"It could actually be a possible bonus because if it makes the party rethink again on the issue of the referendum it could do a power of good," Taylor told Sky Television News.
"The European business has been tearing our party apart for years and the only way we can solve things is to have a referendum and let the people decide," he added.

Labour MPs were reported to be ecstatic about the news, which broke as they ended a regional party conference in Scotland, and some Liberal Democrat sources said they thought another two or three Conservative Eurosceptics might follow Gardiner's example.
Two Conservatives have joined the minority Liberal Democrats in the past year and another quit in October 1995 for the Labour Party.
